interviewQuestions.question: How do you prepare for a remote system design interview differently from an in-person one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I treat tool rehearsal as its own preparation item, separate from practicing the design content itself. If the recruiter tells me the tool in advance, I spend at least ten to fifteen minutes in it beforehand, specifically practicing the handful of actions I'll use constantly — drawing a box, a labeled arrow, adding text, undoing a mistake, and panning the canvas — until they're automatic rather than something I'm hunting for live.

I also test my exact window layout on the actual setup I'll use for the call: whiteboard taking most of the screen, video call visible in a corner so I don't lose the interviewer's nonverbal reactions, and my own notes in a small window I can glance at. I do at least one full mock design under these conditions, ideally with someone watching over a real video call, since drawing alone at my own pace hides friction that only shows up while narrating live.

**Testing:** whether you treat remote mechanics as a distinct preparation item rather than assuming design skill alone transfers unchanged.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Preparing specifically for the remote format

interviewQuestions.question: The interviewer says they can barely read the small text on your diagram. What do you do in the moment?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd acknowledge it immediately and fix it rather than continuing and hoping it's fine going forward: "thanks for flagging that — let me increase the text size and give this more room." I'd then either enlarge the existing text if the tool supports it easily, or, if the canvas is already crowded, move the next section to a fresh, clearly labeled area with more generous spacing from the start.

I'd also use this as a signal to check the rest of the diagram, not just the specific spot mentioned — if one area got cramped, others likely did too, and it's worth a quick scan rather than only patching the one flagged issue.

Going forward for the rest of the interview, I'd deliberately leave more whitespace per box than feels natural, since what looks readable to me at full screen often isn't what the interviewer sees through a compressed video-call view of my screen.

**Testing:** whether you can take real-time feedback about communication mechanics and adjust immediately, not just for the one instance flagged.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Responding to legibility feedback mid-interview

interviewQuestions.question: Your shared whiteboard tool crashes with 20 minutes left in the interview and won't reload. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd say what's happening immediately so the interviewer isn't left guessing: "the whiteboard just crashed on my end — while I try to get it back, let me keep going verbally so we don't lose time." Then I'd switch to the text fallback: describing the remaining architecture as a numbered list of components and a numbered list of the connections between them, which translates more cleanly to spoken or written description than trying to narrate a two-dimensional layout.

If the tool comes back before the interview ends, I'd briefly recap what changed while it was down, rather than assuming the interviewer tracked everything from the verbal description alone, and resume drawing from there.

I wouldn't treat the crash itself as a setback to apologize for at length — most interviewers have seen this before, and how I handle the recovery is what's actually being observed here.

**Testing:** whether you can keep the interview substantively moving through a real technical failure instead of losing the thread or panicking.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Recovering from a whiteboard crash
